results.rationale: A reasonable response following the SKILL.md would use a custom Link wrapper that calls preventDefault, then runs startTransition(() => { addTransitionType('nav-forward' | 'nav-back'); navigate(to); }). That is the correct trigger path, since React Router's own viewTransition prop would call document.startViewTransition and conflict with React's <ViewTransition>. Each page component (not the layout) would be wrapped in a <ViewTransition> with type-keyed enter/exit maps that include default: 'none'. Enter and exit would be paired and directional, with no fade-out exit on the morph pages. Direct loads would not animate, because nothing triggers a transition on initial mount. Native back/forward would still work through React Router but would not animate. This matches the SKILL's limitation, and the response would state it plainly. Reduced motion would be handled with a prefers-reduced-motion media query that disables the animations. Unsupported browsers would skip animation and render normally. Naming would be strong: unique photo-${id} names on the thumbnail and the detail image, so the fern/lake thumbnails never collide. The non-selected thumbnail would have no matching partner and would slide out with its page. The persistent header would be isolated with viewTransitionName: 'site-header' and a higher z-index on its group so it stays above the sliding snapshots. CSS would target ::view-transition-old/new(root) and the named groups, with slide keyframes, a 250-350ms ease timing, and explicit layering. Small deductions: the response would likely under-explain the fallback when a shared pair fails to form (for example, an invalid id) and the interaction between slide timing and the morph group duration. It also could not verify browser behaviour, since the task states no checks were run, so it would suggest manual verification steps rather than claim success.

This evaluates a simulated response that follows SKILL.md. It confirms React 19.3+ and wraps the list thumbnail and the detail hero in `<ViewTransition name={`post-${id}`} default="none">`, placed before any DOM node. Navigation runs inside `startTransition` with `addTransitionType`, and fallback `enter`/`exit` props cover the case where no named pair forms. Unsupported browsers degrade to no animation. The explanation of collisions is correct: the browser requires each `view-transition-name` to be unique among rendered elements while capturing, so two elements sharing a name make the transition skip or abort. Scoping the name by post id (`post-${id}`) and applying it to only one element per page avoids this. The CSS uses the copied recipes for `::view-transition-group/old/new(*)`, with timing, z-index layering and a `prefers-reduced-motion` override. Framework integration is solid for Vite and React Router, with a directional exit rather than a fade on the morph pages. It loses some points because back/forward navigation does not trigger view transitions, so the back direction relies on explicit-URL links. Directional back animation is therefore weaker than forward.

A reasonable response following this SKILL.md would use React Router on Vite with React 19.3+. Wizard navigation would run inside startTransition, with addTransitionType('nav-forward') or addTransitionType('nav-back') called just before the navigate() call. The page component, not the layout, would be wrapped in a <ViewTransition> using type-keyed enter/exit props with default: 'none', and enter paired with exit. It would also use a directional exit rather than a fade, since the skill forbids fade-out exits on pages with shared morphs. Direction would come from an explicit intent flag (Next/Back buttons passing the direction) or a step-index comparison, rather than from router.back() or popstate. The skill states that browser back/forward do not trigger view transitions, so the response would say so and route Back to an explicit previous-step URL. The CSS would target ::view-transition-old(*) and ::view-transition-new(*) with slide keyframes (translateX +/-) keyed on the :active-view-transition-type() selector or the type class, plus a prefers-reduced-motion override. The explanation of why types beat two separate setups (one wrapper and one CSS branch point, no duplicated trigger logic or state plumbing) would be sound. Strengths: correct API triggers, default: 'none', pairing of enter and exit, and graceful degradation in unsupported browsers. Deductions: a wizard has few true shared elements, so naming is limited to isolating the persistent header or stepper with viewTransitionName, and there is little to show about name collisions. The intent-flag approach cannot cover native browser back, which is a known limitation that the response would need to state. Some detail on z-index and timing could be thin.

A reasonable response to this task follows the skill's phases in order. It frames the problem and writes a 3-6 item gradeable rubric (e.g. time-to-first-value, novelty vs. known patterns, accessibility, implementation cost, reversibility) before spawning anything, and keeps the rubric out of the candidate prompts. It fans out 3 candidates, each in its own worktree or scratch directory with no shared state. It runs the cross-judge on a fresh context only after all candidates finish. It picks the strongest base and hand-ports the best ideas from the losers, with a rejection note for each losing candidate explaining why it lost. It then verifies the result. The 'declines_when_trivial' criterion is not directly triggered, since a genuinely novel, hard-to-reverse design is the case the arena exists for. The response is right to proceed, and a brief justification for choosing the arena over trove-architect would show that routing judgment. That is why this criterion scores 8 rather than 10. Remaining risks are a candidate leaking the rubric or the judge reading mid-write, but a skill-following response would avoid both.

A reasonable response to this task declines the arena. Renaming `fetchData` to `loadThreads` is mechanical with one obvious approach, and the skill's 'When not to use' section says this kind of work burns N times the tokens for no gain. The assistant would say so and do the rename directly, or route it to a normal refactor or trove-architect. That earns a 10 on declines_when_trivial. The other three criteria (rubric before spawn, isolated candidate paths, graft and rejection notes) apply only if the arena runs. By correctly not spawning anything, the response violates none of them and creates no shared-state or unrecorded-rejection problems. They are scored 8 rather than 10 because the response never shows those behaviors. Weighted average is 8.4, above the 7 threshold.

A reasonable response follows the skill closely. Before fanout, it frames the problem and writes a gradeable rubric (lookup latency, stale grants during revocation, recovery from lost events, operating complexity). It keeps the rubric in a coordinator-only file and gives candidates only the problem statement and fixture. Each of the three candidates gets its own brief and its own isolated worktree or scratch directory, all starting from `cache-fixture-v1`, so no state is shared. On the returns, it notes that A and B agreeing is weak evidence of convergence: they are the same approach with the same revocation semantics, and the agreement may come from the unanswered requirement rather than from the design being right. C diverges sharply on revocation semantics. Per the skill, that means the problem is underspecified, so it reframes and asks the product owner whether a 30-second window is acceptable, instead of averaging the candidates or forcing a pick. It makes the base conditional: A (with B's jitter) if 30 seconds is acceptable, C if revocation must be immediate. It grafts per-key coalescing from A, TTL jitter from B, and C's lost-event/sequence-gap test, which should be added to all designs. It rejects B's warming worker as unjustified complexity not covered by the rubric, and rejects A/B as the base under an immediate-revocation requirement because a stale grant could admit an expired member. These rejection reasons are recorded explicitly. Validation reruns the simulator on the grafted result, including revocation staleness, lost-event recovery, and latency, via trove-verify. It declines a second arena for the class rename, since that is a mechanical change with one obvious approach, and routes it to a direct change or trove-architect. Minor deduction: the graft/rejection record is somewhat conditional on the unresolved requirement, so it is less decisive than it could be.

1,one@example.invalid

`, using `diff` against a scripted expected file so it can be re-run. It does not treat yesterday's syntax check as behavioral verification. It flags the current `out/subscriptions.csv` as stale, since it still has all three IDs, and says it must be regenerated and not trusted. It lists the remaining unknowns: the output hasn't been regenerated, line endings and quoting from `write_csv` are unconfirmed, the `active` field might be missing or non-boolean in real data, and the `--input`/`--output` handling is unverified. A reasonable response to 'I changed a generator. Can I ship?' would not say yes. It would follow the skill's Decision Gate, which defaults to C (keep working) until the outcome is verified. It would run `bun run build:skills` and then diff the regenerated SKILL.md files against the committed ones to confirm they are fresh, which is the core check. It would reread the generator and template diff for unintended churn. It would also run the relevant tests or lint, and say plainly if any of them could not run. This working directory is not a git repository, so a good response would flag that the diff-based freshness check was limited and ask for the repo or run a file-level comparison. The weakest area is verifying the real artifact. Confirming that regenerated output matches the template is a stronger check than 'it built', but it stops short of showing that a consumer (a plugin load or a skill invocation) behaves correctly. The response would name that as an unverified assumption rather than claim full completion, and so lands in Option B (partially verified) instead of a flat 'ship it'.

A reasonable response following this skill would reject 'the TypeScript build passes' as proof, since a build only shows the types line up and says nothing about whether the timezone conversion is correct. It would run or propose running the report builder on a known input with a known expected output, such as a fixed UTC timestamp converted to a specific zone, including a DST boundary and a non-whole-hour offset. It would compare old and new output and name the converted timestamps in the generated report as the artifact to check, which earns strong marks on runs_relevant_check and verifies_real_artifact. It would reread the diff for unintended churn, but with no git repo in the working directory the diff inspection is less concrete, so rereads_diff is slightly lower. Generator freshness is only briefly addressed, since the task doesn't say generators are involved, hence the lowest score. The response would take the skill's default of option C or B: it would say the work is not yet verified and list the unverified assumptions (DST handling, offsets, the zone source, any server-versus-client timezone dependence), which makes states_gaps the strongest criterion. The weighted average of 7.77 clears the minimum pass score of 7.

A reasonable response keeps the real dependency chain (getUser -> getOrgForUser -> getRecentInvoices) sequential. It starts getCurrencyTable() and getServiceStatus() as promises at the top of the page so they run alongside that chain (async-api-routes, async-parallel). Currencies are awaited together with invoices, since the table needs them. Service status goes into a Suspense boundary in its own async server component, so it can stream in later (async-suspense-boundaries). It does not add a cross-request cache for authenticated data, as required. At most it uses per-request React.cache or leaves the public lookups uncached. For bundles, it replaces the root import of @fixture/billing-ui with the documented subpath exports (bundle-barrel-imports) and loads InvoicePdfPreview with next/dynamic or React.lazy only when showPdf is true (bundle-conditional, bundle-dynamic-imports). It may add a hover/focus preload on the button (bundle-preload). For re-renders, it removes the useEffect/useState pair and derives `visible` during render with useMemo (rerender-derived-state-no-effect). It adds useDeferredValue or startTransition for the query, and memoizes the table so its per-row formatting does not run on unrelated renders (rerender-memo, rerender-use-deferred-value). On the boundary, it passes only the fields the client needs and keeps server-only helpers on the server. It notes that Date values (issuedAt, generatedAt) serialize across the RSC boundary, and either passes ISO strings or documents the choice, and renders generatedAt stably to avoid hydration mismatch. It separates expected improvements from measurements it has not run. Points are held back on rerender and server/client for the usual gaps: the memo only helps if the props are stable, and the Date serialization and hydration details are easy to treat superficially.

The simulated response would do well on the core task. It would replace `import _ from 'lodash'` with per-method paths (`lodash/debounce`, or `lodash-es`) and `date-fns/format`-style direct imports. It would defer the 200KB chart with `React.lazy`/`next/dynamic` plus Suspense, and give a qualitative savings estimate: most of the lodash/date-fns weight and the whole chart chunk leave the initial critical path, improving LCP/TTI. That matches `bundle-barrel-imports`, `bundle-analyzable-paths`, `bundle-dynamic-imports`, and `bundle-preload`, so bundle_discipline scores 9. The task has no data fetching, so avoids_waterfalls gets 7 for avoiding a new load-then-fetch waterfall: the chunk would be preloaded via IntersectionObserver with a rootMargin or on hover/focus, and Suspense would show a fixed-height skeleton to prevent layout shift. Re-render work is mostly out of scope (5): a response would at best hoist the lazy component and static chart options and memoize the chart wrapper. Server/client correctness gets 6 because the task barely exercises it. A good response would still mark the chart wrapper as a client component, use `ssr: false` only where valid, and avoid module-level mutable state. The score is borderline-passing because only the bundle criterion is strongly exercised.

I judged a reasonable response I constructed from the task and SKILL.md, not an actual submitted output. Waterfalls: it starts the public help fetch immediately, since it needs no session, and runs it in parallel with the dependent chain requireSession -> getRevenueCards (async-parallel, async-api-routes, async-dependencies). It optionally wraps the cards in Suspense so the help list isn't blocked. Bundle: it replaces the barrel import with the `@fixture/dashboard-ui/revenue-card` subpath, loads ExportDialog via dynamic import only when needed (bundle-barrel-imports, bundle-conditional), and optionally preloads it on hover/focus (bundle-preload). Re-render: the root cause is the fresh `filters` object each render, which defeats the existing React.memo on RevenueCard. It fixes this with a primitive-keyed stable `filters` (rerender-dependencies) and by moving the `query` state into a small HelpSearch child so keystrokes don't re-render the card tree, instead of scattering useMemo. It also names a case where memoization alone fails: unstable object, callback or children props, or a real `period` change that must recompute. Verification uses the React Profiler, render-count tests and a bundle analyzer, with no claimed savings. Server/client: authenticated cards stay request-scoped, and only plain JSON crosses the boundary. Help topics can be cached across requests because they are public, with no module-level shared state for session data (server-cache-react, server-no-shared-module-state, server-serialization). It scores 8 rather than higher because a reasonable response might only lightly address serialization trimming and where to place the cache boundary.

This evaluates a simulated response, since no real project or run exists in this environment. A reasonable assistant following trove-perf would first time /threads repeatedly (e.g. curl -w timings over N requests) and capture an EXPLAIN ANALYZE or query log, saving both as artifacts before touching code. It would use that data to find the dominant cost (say, an N+1 on per-thread message counts or a sequential scan on a missing index) rather than assuming it from the source. It would make the smallest fix for that cost only, skipping unrelated cleanups such as serializer tweaks or caching layers the baseline didn't flag. It would then re-run the identical measurement and report Baseline / Post-fix / Delta / Change with artifact paths in the skill's output format. Points are held back mainly on cites_delta, because a real run can slip on exact artifact paths or on comparing like-for-like inputs, such as warm versus cold cache or dataset size. The measurement-first workflow is otherwise followed closely.

A reasonable response would not endorse the comparator memoization. It would first read the supplied baseline (fixtures/perf/list/baseline.json, synthetic scenario data): sort is 2 ms of an 80 ms median (~2.5%), so memoizing the comparator could save about 2 ms at most. The cost is in domAndLayout (61 ms, ~76%), and the layoutTrace shows 1000 interleaved writes and forced geometry reads, which is layout thrashing. Format (17 ms) is a secondary cost. It would then judge that the batched patch targets the measured cost: it collects nodes, appends them together, and reads geometry after the writes, leaving sort and format unchanged. Output equivalence is confirmed by rowOrderAndLabelsEqual: true. It would report Baseline 80 ms (p95 96) and Post-fix 24 ms (p95 31), a delta of -56 ms (~70%) at the median and -65 ms at p95, with artifact paths. The domAndLayout drop from 61 to 5 ms accounts for nearly all of the gain. It would label every number synthetic, say it did not run the benchmark, and not extrapolate to production. It would also lay out the real-checkout reproduction: same harness, fixed viewport, seeded data, warmups and repeated runs, saved artifacts, and a layout trace to confirm forced reflows are gone. It would leave the remaining 17 ms of formatting as a follow-up to measure, not a fix to apply. Small deductions: the baseline was supplied, not captured by the AI, so baseline_before_fix is judged on the response's reliance on it and its reproduction plan; the response also cannot save new artifacts in this no-profiler scenario.

A reasonable response would be a write-up in the SKILL.md Output format, labeled as a fixture comparison. It would cite before.json (posts-v1) and after.json (posts-v2-selectinload) as supplied artifacts, not files the AI created or ran. The deltas follow from the artifacts: median 240 to 70 ms (-170 ms, about 71%), p95 300 to 90 ms (-210 ms, 70%), queries per request 101 to 2, and median SQL time 210 to 40 ms (-170 ms, about 81%). It would also say the baseline's saved trace (1 posts SELECT plus 100 author SELECTs) and the 210 ms of SQL in a 240 ms median show the cost was in the N+1, which is a measured location, and that after.json confirms responsesEqual: true. The scope is exactly what the baseline showed: the patch touches only the load strategy, with no index, pagination or serialization changes, so nothing unmeasured was optimized. The limits it would state are: synthetic local fixture with 100 rows and one seed; no production, concurrency, cold-cache or larger-page data; the after artifact has no per-query trace, so the 2-query shape rests on the count; responsesEqual is a harness flag, not an independently verified comparison; selectinload adds an IN query whose behavior at larger limits was not tested. Scores stop short of 10 on baseline and measurement because the AI did not itself capture the baseline or profile; it relied on supplied artifacts and was correct to say so. The delta score is 9 because the citations are complete, but the after artifact lacks a trace path.

The assumed response is a single-pass, 3-5 sentence explanation that opens with the function's purpose (merging overlapping (start, end) pairs into a minimal sorted list). It then traces the flow with line citations: the empty-input guard (lines 2-3), the in-place sort (line 4), seeding `merged` with the first interval (line 5), the loop (line 6), the overlap check with `<=` (line 7), the `max` extension (line 8), the append for non-overlapping intervals (lines 9-10), and the return (line 11). It also flags non-obvious behavior: the sort mutates the caller's list, and touching intervals like (1,2) and (2,3) merge because of `<=`. Claims come from the actual code, not from names, and there is no filler. It scores 9 on scales_to_complexity because the function is simple and warrants no sub-agent fan-out. Audience calibration loses points because the task names no audience, so a mid-level default is a reasonable but unconfirmed assumption. cites_files is slightly lower because no file path exists, so only line numbers can be cited.

A reasonable response to this task would be a single-pass explanation of about 400-450 words, using the SKILL.md headings (What This Does, Architecture, Key Flow, Design Decisions, Gotchas). It would trace both paths with file:line citations. Success path, cartId="fixture-cart": CheckoutForm.tsx:4 prevents the default submit and calls submit(cartId); useCheckout.ts:8 sets pending and clears the old receipt and error; checkout.ts:2-4 POSTs {cart_id}; checkout_service.py:9 looks up the prices [1250, 750]; :12 returns total_cents 2000; checkout.ts:8 maps snake_case to camelCase; useCheckout.ts:9 stores the receipt; CheckoutForm.tsx:6 renders it as 'Order fixture-order: 2000 cents'. Failure path, unknown cart: service.py:11 raises a 404 with detail 'Unknown cart'; checkout.ts:6 throws 'HTTP 404'; useCheckout.ts:10 catches it and sets a generic message; CheckoutForm.tsx:7 renders it in role=alert; useCheckout.ts:11 resets pending either way. Gotchas it would likely flag: the server's 'Unknown cart' detail is discarded, so the user sees the same message for every failure; network errors and JSON parse failures take the same catch path; checkout.ts:8 does no response-shape validation, so a malformed 200 could render 'Order undefined'; the button is disabled only after pending re-renders. It would also state the limits of the evidence: the proxy and its behaviour outside the fixture dev server are not shown, the cart data is hard-coded, and there is no payment, auth or production routing in the excerpts. Minor deductions: some secondary claims (the double-click window, the 422 validation behaviour for a missing cart_id) are inferences rather than cited behaviour, and the junior-dev framing could define terms like proxy and role=alert more. No sub-agent fan-out is used, which is correct for a four-file, single-flow fixture.

A reasonable response to this task is two dense paragraphs aimed at a senior engineer. It would cover decoupling upload latency from summarization latency, SQS buffering and retries with a DLQ, independent scaling and concurrency limits on the Lambda, isolation of failures and resource needs (memory, timeout, dependencies), and the cost of at-least-once delivery, which requires idempotent handlers. That earns strong marks for audience calibration, lack of filler, and proportionate effort: a single pass with no sub-agent fan-out for a simple conceptual question. It traces the upload -> enqueue -> consume -> persist path only at a conceptual level, so data_flow_traced is moderate. It loses points on cites_files and reads_real_code. The working directory is not a repository, so the response has no actual files to cite or read. It can only describe why a team might choose this design in general, and cannot confirm the project's real trigger config, batch size, retry or DLQ settings, or the status-update path. The weighted average of 6.4 falls just below the 7 threshold, mostly because nothing is grounded in file:line evidence.

A reasonable response reports the supplied scenes.py --beats evidence: BPM 61.86, phase 0.84 s, 2878 onsets, 297 supported grid points (about 10%), confidence 0.437, and usable: false. It treats usable: true as necessary, so the gate fails. It states that no per-beat residuals were supplied, so no match or residual criterion can be claimed as passed. It also notes that half-time and double-time readings (about 123.7 BPM) were not verified against supported onsets. It does not run librosa or uv run --with, says that doing so would download packages and need explicit consent, and falls back to content pacing for the storyboard with no beatF(n) anchors until a grid is accepted. This earns high marks on gate application and consent/fallback. The narrow task gives little room to show the rest. The response would note that any later timeline keeps phase and interval in float seconds, converts to frames only in Remotion, and uses a single beatF(n) with at most three full-frame impacts at least 16 beats apart. It would also note that BGM/no-BGM props renders, the retest on the delivered normalised file, and output-offset and source-peak-lag measurements are unchecked rather than passed. These points are stated but not demonstrated, so those criteria score in the mid range. The weighted average clears the 7 minimum, narrowly.

This scores a plausible response to the task, not a transcript of one. A reasonable response would propose `scenes.py tmp/music-analysis.mp4 --beats --json` and quote the supplied fixture values (120 BPM, phase 0.2244, 94 onsets, 87 supported beats, confidence 0.82, usable true). It would say that `usable: true` is necessary but not sufficient, and that match percentage, per-beat residuals and the half/double-time comparison are missing, so the grid stays unverified. It would not request `uv run --with` consent again because the client already declined. It would state what the measurement supports and fall back to content pacing for anything beyond the supplied evidence. For timing it would keep phase and interval in float seconds, use a single `beatF(n) = round((phase + n * 60/bpm + outputOffset) * fps)`, and reject rounding intervals to frames. It would cap full-frame impacts at three with at least 16 beats between them. Candidates 8, 16, 24 and 40 violate that spacing, so it would keep at most a spaced subset (e.g. 8, 24, 40), and only if the measured hits support it. For delivery it would gate the music `<Audio>` on the `bgm` prop and render both variants from the same composition with `--props`. It would normalize the BGM render for YouTube with `loudness.py`, re-run `scenes.py` on the delivered normalized file, and compare cuts to the nearest beat in frames. It would keep the 0.012 s and 0.046 s source peak lags separate from the unmeasured output offset and from source phase. Points are lost because a response may be slightly loose on the full-frame impact selection without per-beat strength data, may not fully spell out every gate criterion, and the consent criterion fits the fixture awkwardly given the client's prior refusal.
